title: DROP TABLE & CASCADE Behavior
description: Safely remove tables, manage foreign key cascades with CASCADE vs RESTRICT, and verify IF EXISTS.

data.text: The **`DROP TABLE`** statement permanently removes a table, its data, associated indexes, and triggers from the database.

data.title: DROP TABLE with CASCADE
data.content: Dropping a table and all dependent views or foreign keys automatically.

data.text: A table that other objects depend on — a foreign key from a child table, a view, a materialized view — cannot be dropped until those dependencies are gone. By default `DROP TABLE` uses `RESTRICT`, which **refuses** and tells you what depends on it. `CASCADE` silently removes the dependent objects too, which can delete far more than you intended.

data.title: Discovering Dependencies Before You Drop
data.code:
-- What depends on this table?
SELECT DISTINCT dependent.relname AS dependent_object,
       dependent.relkind,
       pg_get_userbyid(dependent.relowner) AS owner
FROM pg_depend d
JOIN pg_class dependent ON dependent.oid = d.objid
JOIN pg_class source    ON source.oid    = d.refobjid
WHERE source.relname = 'categories' AND source.relkind = 'r';

-- Restrict (default): fails if anything depends on the table
DROP TABLE categories;                      -- ERROR: cannot drop: other objects depend on it

-- Cascade: removes dependent views and foreign keys as well
DROP TABLE categories CASCADE;

-- Idempotent form used in scripts
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS obsolete_logs;

-- Drop several objects in one statement
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS a, b, c RESTRICT;

data.text: `TRUNCATE` is far faster than `DELETE` because it deallocates whole pages instead of writing one WAL record per row, and it resets nothing about the sequence unless you add `RESTART IDENTITY`. `DELETE` leaves dead tuples behind for `VACUUM`.

data.title: There Is No `UNDROP TABLE`
data.text: Dropping is transactional, so `BEGIN; DROP TABLE t; ROLLBACK;` is safe — but once committed the data is gone. In production the safe workflow is: rename (`ALTER TABLE t RENAME TO t_dropped_20260101;`) and drop it after a retention window, or restore the table from a logical/physical backup.

items.question: What is the difference between `DROP` and `DELETE`?
items.answer: `DELETE` removes rows and leaves the table structure; `DROP` removes the whole object. `DELETE` is row-by-row and logged for replication, `DROP` is a catalog operation.

items.question: When would you use `TRUNCATE`?
items.answer: For bulk clearing where you want speed and do not need row-level triggers to fire (though `TRUNCATE` triggers do exist) — for example, resetting a staging table between loads.

items.question: Does `DROP TABLE` free disk space?
items.answer: It removes the files, so yes, the OS reclaims the space. `DELETE` and `DROP COLUMN` do not immediately — the space is reused internally after `VACUUM`.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `DROP TABLE` defaults to `RESTRICT`; `CASCADE` follows and removes dependent views and foreign keys as well.
Investigate dependencies in `pg_depend`/`pg_class` before dropping anything with `CASCADE`.
`DELETE`, `TRUNCATE`, and `DROP` differ in scope, speed, locks, and transactional behaviour.
Production-safe deletion is usually a rename plus a delayed drop, not an immediate drop.
